lead: A feedforward network sees one input and forgets it. Many problems are sequences: words in a sentence, frames of a video, a sensor reading each second. A recurrent neural network (RNN) keeps a small vector called the hidden state, which carries what the network has seen so far. At each step it mixes the new input with the old state. One cell and one set of weights serve every time step. Language modelling, speech recognition and video tagging all start here.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 for tanh and matrix multiplication, and 4.1 for how a sequence is written x₁ … x_T and padded into batches.

blocks.text: A sequence is x₁, x₂, …, x_T, one vector per step (see 4.1). A feedforward layer would treat each xt alone, with no idea what came before. An RNN adds one thing: a hidden state that travels from step to step.
h<sub>t</sub> = tanh(W<sub>xh</sub> x<sub>t</sub> + W<sub>hh</sub> h<sub>t−1</sub> + b<sub>h</sub>),   y<sub>t</sub> = W<sub>hy</sub> h<sub>t</sub> + b<sub>y</sub>
blocks.where: x<sub>t</sub> is the input vector at step t of length d (shape B×d for a batch of B sequences); h<sub>t</sub> is the hidden state of length H, the number of hidden units (shape B×H); W<sub>xh</sub> is the input-to-hidden matrix of shape d×H; W<sub>hh</sub> is the recurrent matrix of shape H×H; b<sub>h</sub> is a bias vector of length H; W<sub>hy</sub> is H×k and b<sub>y</sub> is length k, giving output y<sub>t</sub> of length k; tanh acts element by element and squashes values into (−1, 1). For k-class prediction, apply softmax to y<sub>t</sub>.

blocks.text: The same three matrices are used at every step. Step 1 and step 100 share W<sub>xh</sub>, W<sub>hh</sub> and W<sub>hy</sub>. That sharing is the whole point: the model learns one rule for mixing past and present, and applies it however long the sequence runs.

h<sub>0</sub> has no step before it, so you initialise it yourself, usually to a zero vector of shape B×H. Some books write U for W<sub>hh</sub>, W for W<sub>xh</sub> and V for W<sub>hy</sub>. The letters change; the equation does not. This cell is commonly called the vanilla RNN or the simple RNN. Both names are standard, so use either one in an answer.
Draw the cell once per time step and connect the copies. That picture is the unfolded RNN.

See the figure. x(t) and h(t−1) enter the cell, tanh mixes them, and h(t) leaves. One copy of h(t) goes to the output head; another goes to the next step. The arrow from h(t) to h(t+1) carries exactly the same matrix as the arrow from h(t−1) to h(t). Unfolding adds no parameters. It is the same model, drawn deep.

Why draw it? After unfolding, the network is an ordinary feedforward graph whose depth equals the sequence length T, and gradient descent on such a graph is ordinary backpropagation. That training pass is called backpropagation through time and is the subject of 4.3.

The picture also shows the cost. Each step multiplies the input by a d×H matrix, the state by an H×H matrix, and the result by an H×k output matrix. A forward pass over T steps is about O(T·(d·H + H·H + H·k)) multiply-adds; ignoring the small output head, the recurrent part is O(T·H·(d+H)). Long sequences cost more, and their gradients stretch back further; the gated cells of 4.4 exist to handle the second problem.
The recurrent body, the chain of hidden states, is the same in every task. What changes is where you read the output and how many steps you run.

items: Many-to-one: run T steps, read y only at the last step. Use it for the sentiment of a review or a label for a video clip.
One-to-many: feed one input, such as an image vector from a CNN, then keep the state running with dummy inputs and emit a word at each step. Use it for image captioning.
Many-to-many, aligned: emit y<sub>t</sub> at every step, as in part-of-speech tagging where input and output have equal length.

Many-to-many, shifted: read the whole input, then emit an output of a different length one token at a time, feeding the previous output back as the next input. This is the encoder-decoder pattern of 4.5.

blocks.text: For video, a CNN from Unit 3 turns each frame into a feature vector; the RNN then consumes those vectors in order and predicts a label or a caption.

One more variant: a bidirectional RNN runs two cells, one left to right and one right to left, and concatenates their states at each step. Then h<sub>t</sub> depends on past and future inputs. That helps tagging, but it cannot be used for step-by-step generation, where the future does not exist yet.

figure.caption: The same cell drawn at three steps: x(t) and h(t−1) are mixed into h(t), which feeds the output y(t) and the next copy of the cell. The dashed arrow reuses the same recurrent matrix, so unfolding adds no new parameters.

spec.title: Unfolded RNN
spec.aria: The same hidden cell is reused at three time steps: x(t) and h(t-1) form h(t), which gives y(t) and passes to h(t+1).

examples.question: A scalar RNN has W_xh = 1, W_hh = 0.5, b_h = 0, W_hy = 1, b_y = 0 and h_0 = 0. The inputs are x_1 = 1 and x_2 = 2. Compute h_1, h_2 and y_2, rounded to two decimals.
steps: Write the scalar equations: h_t = tanh(1·x_t + 0.5·h_{t−1}) and y_t = 1·h_t + 0.
Step 2: the input term is 1×2 = 2.000; the state term is 0.5×0.7616 = 0.3808; their sum is 2.3808. h_2 = tanh(2.3808) = 0.9830, so h_2 ≈ 0.98.
examples.answer: h_1 = 0.76, h_2 = 0.98 and y_2 = 0.98, to two decimals.
examples.check:
import math
h1 = math.tanh(1*1 + 0.5*0)
h2 = math.tanh(1*2 + 0.5*h1)
y2 = 1*h2 + 0
print(round(h1, 2))
print(round(h2, 2))
print(round(y2, 2))

traps: h_t at each time step is not a separate learned parameter. Only W_xh, W_hh, W_hy, b_h and b_y are learned; h_t is computed.
h_0 must be initialised. A zero vector is the usual choice; leaving it undefined makes the first step impossible.
Do not confuse h_t, the internal state, with y_t, the output. The state is passed forward; the output is what the loss is computed on.
Shape slip: W_hh is H×H, not d×H, because it multiplies h_{t−1} of length H. In a batch, h_t has shape B×H and y_t has shape B×k.
tanh is not sigmoid. tanh(0) = 0 and the range is (−1, 1); sigmoid(0) = 0.5 and the range is (0, 1). Examiners test this.

quiz.q: Write the RNN update equation and name each symbol.
quiz.a: h_t = tanh(W_xh x_t + W_hh h_{t−1} + b_h). x_t is the input at step t, h_t the hidden state, W_xh the input-to-hidden weights, W_hh the recurrent weights, b_h the bias.

quiz.q: What is h_0 and how is it set?
quiz.a: It is the hidden state before the first input. It has no predecessor, so it is initialised by hand, usually to a zero vector of length H (shape B×H in a batch).

quiz.q: Why does an RNN share weights across time?
quiz.a: One learned rule must work at any position and any sequence length. Sharing keeps the parameter count fixed (d×H + H×H + H×k plus biases) and lets the model generalise to lengths not seen in training.

quiz.q: What information does h_t carry, and what limits it?
quiz.a: A compressed summary of x₁ … x_t. It is a fixed-length vector, so distant detail fades, and repeated multiplication by W_hh shrinks gradients during backpropagation (see 4.3).

quiz.q: A scalar RNN has W_xh = 2, W_hh = 0.5, b_h = 0, h_0 = 0 and x_1 = 1. Find h_1 to two decimals.
A batch has B = 32 sequences, input length d = 100, H = 128 hidden units and k = 10 output classes. Give the shapes of W_xh, W_hh, W_hy, h_t and y_t.
A sentiment classifier and a translation model both use an RNN body. Which output head does each need, and why?
quiz.a: Sentiment gives one label for the whole review: many-to-one, reading the output only at the last step. Translation emits a sequence of a different length: encoder-decoder, reading the source and then generating one token at a time with the previous output fed back (4.5).

quiz.q: Why can a bidirectional RNN help part-of-speech tagging but not step-by-step generation?
quiz.a: It concatenates a left-to-right and a right-to-left state, so h_t sees future inputs as well as past ones. At generation time the future tokens do not exist yet, so only the left-to-right pass is available.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production NLP, recurrence has largely been replaced by attention and Transformers (Unit 5), because the unfolded graph parallelises badly over long sequences. Recurrence survives where data arrives one step at a time: streaming sensors, on-device speech, and video models that pair a CNN per frame with a recurrent head. Newer state-space models such as S4 and Mamba bring back a linear recurrence and keep the unfolding idea, but replace W_hh by a structured, often diagonal, matrix. Search next for "backpropagation through time", "truncated BPTT" and "state space models".
